However, while these methods are crucial for regulatory purposes, they have certain limitations, including the requirement for predefined quantification targets and the restricted availability of reference standards. These constraints limit detection to only a small fraction of PFASs — just a few dozen out of the thousands that may be present. To address this limitation, a more comprehensive approach to PFAS identification and quantification in complex impacted water is needed. The adsorption capacities of short-chain PFAS across different sorbents remain limited compared to their long-chain homologues because of their low hydrophobicity. In general, carbon-based sorbents are more effective in the removal of long-chain PFAS, since the adsorption process is highly dominated by hydrophobic interactions. selected_context.text: The long-term viability of adsorption-based treatment systems for PFAS-contaminated water depends not only on removal efficiency but also on how adsorbents are regenerated, managed and ultimately disposed of at the end of their service life. This review highlights that while notable progress has been made, no single regeneration method offers a universal solution. Thermal regeneration remains the most established approach, particularly for carbon-based adsorbents, but its high energy demand and potential structural damage con- strain its wider application. Solvent- and chemical-based methods achieve strong recovery and, in some cases, good multi-cycle stability, yet their benefits are offset by the generation of PFAS-contaminated liquid wastes requiring downstream treatment. Emerging electro- chemical and hybrid techniques show promise by combining desorption with partial in situ degradation, but their technical feasibility, durability and economic viability at scale remain uncertain. When regeneration is no longer viable, the disposal or destruction of PFAS- saturated adsorbents remains challenging. High-temperature incineration is currently the most reliable route for near-complete PFAS mineralisation but is limited by cost, energy de- mand and the risk of incomplete destruction. Alternative oxidative or chemical destruction approaches are under development but have yet to demonstrate large-scale performance, and immobilisation and stabilisation techniques offer only interim containment rather than permanent elimination.

One sustainable approach in - volves stabilizing or solidifying spent CFA, which can immobilize con - taminants and reduce the risk of leaching when disposed of in controlled landfills. Alternatively, spent CFA could be repurposed in construction materials, such as cement or concrete, if it meets regulatory standards for leachability. This reuse strategy not only reduces waste but also substitutes for traditional materials with a recycled byproduct, lowering the carbon footprint of construction applications. In some cases, thermal or chemical regeneration could restore CFA ’ s adsorptive capacity, enabling its reuse for PFAS adsorption, although the environmental and economic feasibility of regeneration methods must be carefully evalu - ated. Ultimately, a sustainable approach to CFA handling requires a combination of effective waste stabilization, potential material repur - pose, and regulatory compliance to ensure long-term environmental safety. 4. Conclusion • CFA is a feasible option to remove organic matter and PFAS from landfill leachate and other wastewater as an alternative adsorbent to the widely used carbon-based adsorbents. • Acid and thermal modification of CFA is necessary to enhance its adsorbing properties, increasing BET surface area by 2.5-3.5 times and pore volume by 2-3 times.

In these cases, the treatment meth- odology is multistep requiring additional expenditure of energy along with cost associated with complexity. Direct decomposition is desirable in that ideally it does not create an additional waste stream; rather, the compound is disassembled chemically to harm- less by-products. Key questions regarding PFAS treatment include what is the fate of the shorter chains produced, and is the advanced method also appropriate to treat these shorter chains? Such ques- tions have not been settled to date. 8 In this work, plasma treatment is applied to the treatment of PFAS-contaminated ground water. While plasma treatment is often thought of as an advanced oxidation method, it has been shown that oxidation is not effective in decomposing short chain PFAS compounds. 8 This is largely due the relative strength of the C –F bond and the high electronegativity of fluorine. The oxidation potential of fluorine is larger than that of OH, the chief radical in advanced oxidation. Reduction methods, on the other hand, have shown success at defluorinating and ultimately decomposing PFAS compounds. 9 These methods feature solvated electrons —a short lived, highly reactive complex that destabilizes PFAS compounds.

Ion-exchange resins are among the most widely applied polymeric materials for PFAS remediation due to their robust electrostatic interactions with anionic PFASs. Structural variations among resins, such as gel-type v. macroporous configurations, affect mass transfer kinetics and adsorption capacity. selected_context.text: AORP methods (photocatalysis, EAOP , NTP , E- beam), pyrolysis, and SCWO have been proposed to achieve the final destruction of PFAS compounds. Ongoing research aims at reducing the cost of these technologies and improving their destruction efficiency; commercial PFAS destruction methods have been introduced recently, but their full-scale application is still unreported in the scientific literature. Concerns about the potential for some PFASs and precursors to break through current treatment methods, the partial degradation of targeted compounds to non-targeted ones, and potentially dangerous by-products have not been dismissed yet, due to the non- detectability of a large number of PFAS molecules beyond those targeted by regulations. Incomplete and uncertain degradation pathways following destructive treatment also raise issues about overall risk reduction. A major challenge for the assessment of an effective reduction in PFAS contamination is related to the standardization of their quantification methodologies and to the development of analytical advancements to allow for the identification of PFAS congeners following specific treatments and fine-tune both removal and destructive remediation technologies. Generally speaking, the most effective technologies for breaking down PFASs are those that can rapidly deliver high energy into a contaminated solution, in order to overcome the high C-F bond strength and avoid by-product accumulation during the destruction process.

Thus, the ability of membrane technologies to remove PFAS in water and wastewater systems is a promising research and application topic [ 10 , 23 ]. Membrane separation processes are widely applied in water/waste - water treatment and industries and it was found to be effective in rejecting short and long chain PFAS with efficiencies exceeding 90 % [ 24 , 25 ]. Generally, in membrane separation systems, feed water con - taining PFAS molecules is rejected by the membrane (semi-permeable selective barrier) while water molecules are passing to the permeation side of the system. The most famous, effective and largely investigated membrane systems for PFAS removal are pressure driven membrane systems, particularly nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) sys - tems. The defined removal mechanism are size exclusion, electrostatic repulsion and solution diffusion for NF and RO, respectively. The effi - ciency of these membranes in rejecting PFASs from aqueous environ - ments were reported to approach 99 % [ 26 , 27 ]. Despite the maturity level of the NF and RO systems and simplicity in application, the major drawback experienced is treatment of rejected streams containing high PFAS concentration which requires further attention by coupling membrane separation with other processes such as adsorption or AOPs.

It is widely recognized that the negatively charged PFAS molecules are typically repelled from the cathode. 18,19 For example, a study clearly showed a three -order-of-magnitude drop in the PFOA partition coefficient between the aqueous phase and the Au surface when a negative potential was applied. 15 Noticeable cathodic PFOS adsorption has previously been observed only on carbon nanotubes functionalized with cationic surfactants, where electrostatic attraction between the anionic PFOS headgroups and positively charged surfactant layers occurs.12 Even with successful PFAS adsorption on the cathode, achieving reduct ive defluorination is challenging . Through ﬂuoridation and amination of poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA), the newly synthesized sorbents can sorb the ﬁve targeted PFASs (perﬂuorooctanoic acid (PFOA), per ﬂuorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), per ﬂuorobutanesulfonic acid (PFBS), and per ﬂuor- obutanoic acid (PFBA) and GenX) to di ﬀerent degrees from aqueous solution. Aminated PEGDA showed the highest sorption capacity for all ﬁve PFASs, particularly for PFBA and PFBS. The bifunctionalized PEGDA showed higher capacities for PFOA and PFOS, suggesting that both hydrophobic interactions and charges contribute to the sorption. Both aminated and bifunctionalized sorbents can remove GenX from water, with the highest sorption capacity of 98.7 μmol g aminated PEGDA −1 within 6 h. The absorbed PFASs on the sorbents were observed and characterized by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy. The spent sorbents were reusable after readily regenerated with 70% methanol contained 1% NaCl. ■ INTRODUCTION Per- and poly ﬂuoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are groups of synthetic compounds with low surface tension and unique hydrophobic and hydrophilic characteristics. PFASs are broadly used in various industries, including paintings, clothing, electrical conductors, and polytetra ﬂuoroethylene coatings for many decades. 1 Exposure to PFASs has been demonstrated to cause developmental e ﬀects, liver and kidney toxicity, immune e ﬀects, and cancer in animal studies.

Accordingly, we hypothesize that PEGDA- based hydrogel sorbents can be functionalized using 1H,1H,2H,2H-perﬂuorooctyl methacrylate (13FOMA) and [2-(methacryloyloxy)ethyl]trimethylammonium chloride solu- tion (MTAC) to create hydrophobic regions and/or electro- static attractive interaction. In this study, the functionalization of PEGDA is achieved by amination, ﬂuoridation, and bifunctionalization ( Figure 1 ). The amination of PEGDA contributes electrostatic force, whereas the ﬂuoridation of PEGDA presents the hydrophobic interaction. The bifunction- alization of PEGDA integrates amination and ﬂuoridation, which contributes electrostatic force and hydrophobic interaction simultaneously. This work is aimed at evaluating their performance for removing long-chain (PFOA and PFOS), short-chain ﬂuorinated substances (PFBA and PFBS), and per ﬂuoroalkyl ether carboxylic acid group (GenX) from the water. selected_context.text: Review Sorptive removal of per- and poly ﬂuoroalkyl substances from aqueous solution: Enhanced sorption, challenges and perspectives Hao Yu, Hao Chen, Bo Fang, Hongwen Sun ⁎ MOE Key Laboratory of Pollution Processes and Environmental Criteria, College of Environmental Science and Engineering, Nankai University, Tianjin 300350, China HIGHLIGHTS GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT  Polymers remove short-chain PFASs more efﬁciently than other sorbents.  Newly developed functionalized sorbents can substantially enhance PFAS sorption.  Composite materials show synergistic ef- fects compared to single materials.  Newly pathways such as air-water interfa- cial adsorption can enhance PFAS sorption.  Steric design based on PFAS molecular size can enhance selective removal of PFASs. ABSTRACTARTICLE INFO Editor: Jay Gan Keywords: Long- and short-chain PFASs Sorption Sorption mechanisms Sorbents AFFF-impacted water Per- and polyﬂuoroalkyl substances (PFASs) have garnered attention globally given their ubiquitous occurrence, tox- icity, bioaccumulative potential, and environmental persistence. Sorption is widely used to remove PFASs given its simplicity and cost-effectiveness. This article reviews recently fabricated sorbents, including carbon materials, min- erals, polymers, and composite materials. The characteristics and interactions of the sorbents with PFASs are discussed to better understand sorptive processes. Various sorbents have exhibited high removal rates for legacy perﬂuorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perﬂuorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS).

Numerous studies have employed bed volumes (BV(s)) to breakthrough behavior as a focal point of adsorbent evaluation [18,30,38] . However, this form of comparison is obscured by different BV sizes, operating conditions, and high concentrations of adsorbates impacting the avail - ability of adsorption sites. Without a comprehensive metric for treat - ment comparison, treatment selection between multiple adsorbents in highly complex matrices is difficult and further exacerbated by the dearth of information associated with the direct application of adsor - bents at full-scale applications. With limited available information comparing PFAS removal effectiveness in waters with elevated con - centrations of DOC and inorganic ions inhibiting PFAS removal, the need for pretreatment strategies or elongated contact time to reduce adsorbent use rates has yet to be investigated. Application of breakthrough modeling using the Thomas model, as previously applied by Schaefer et al. [24] and Grieco et al. [23] , alle - viates the challenges associated with evaluating adsorbent performance and pretreatment necessity by distilling breakthrough curves into model parameters. selected_context.text: Water treatment Adsorption Breakthrough modeling ABSTRACT Granular activated carbon (GAC) has proven to be a successful technology for per- and polyfluoroalkyl sub - stances (PFAS) removal from contaminated drinking water supplies. Proper design of GAC treatment relies upon characterization of media service-life, which can change significantly depending on the PFAS contamination, treatment media, and water quality, and is often determined by fitting descriptive models to breakthrough curves. However, while common descriptive breakthrough models are favored for their ease-of-use, they have a significant shortcoming in that they are not able to properly fit PFAS desorption in competitive sorption sce - narios. The present work adapts three common descriptive models to fit competitive PFAS breakthrough curves from a GAC pilot study. The adapted and original models were fit to the experimental breakthrough curves for 12 common PFAS and evaluated using adjusted R 2 and reduced χ 2 values. This study found that the novel adaptation of the common descriptive models successfully accounted for desorption of PFAS compounds from the GAC, accurately describing increased exposure risks due to elevated effluent levels during desorption without signif - icantly increasing the complexity of implementing the models. * Corresponding author at: Institute for Water Technology and Policy, Stantec, Washington DC 20005, USA. E-mail address: joseph.jacangelo@stantec.com (J.G. Jacangelo).

selected_context.text: Among the tested adsorbents, AC functionalized with 1% CTAB demonstrated good removal efficiency (>90%) for both short-chain and long-chain PFCAs. Its performance was also comparable to that of the commercial ion exchange resins. In contrast, AC and alginate hydrogels exhibited significant adsorption only for PFOA (85 ± 6.9%), with considerably lower removal efficiencies for short-chain PFCAs (19.56 ± 5.4%). Since short chain PFCAs are primarily removed via electrostatic interaction rather than hydrophobic interaction, their improved removal performance upon CTAB impregnation in the AC implies enhanced electrostatic interaction due to the quaternary ammonium group with the PFCAs. However, it is also noticed that despite CTAB functionalization, the alginate hydrogels did not show comparable performance to the CTAB-functionalized AC. This highlights the importance of the background framework for PFAS-selective functionalization using species such as CTAB. Since the background alginate framework in the hydrogel is hydrophilic and the presence of negatively charged functional groups, such as carboxyl and hydroxyl, can induce electrostatic repulsion between the adsorbent surface and the short chain PFCAs, the effective adsorption of short-chain PFCAs by the hydrogel was lower than the corresponding CTAB- functionalized AC. Based on the adsorption performance, 1% CTAB-functionalized AC was selected for further investigations in this study.

selected_context.text: Conclusion This review summarizes and critically evaluates the sorption capacities of different sorbents for the removal of both long- and short-chain PFAS from aqueous solutions. Carbonaceous materials, namely GAC and PAC, in addition to resins are the most widely used sorbents for PFAS remediation. The adsorption capacities of short-chain PFAS across different sorbents remain limited compared to their long-chain homologues because of their low hydrophobicity. In general, carbon-based sorbents are more effective in the removal of long-chain PFAS, since the adsorption process is highly dominated by hydrophobic interactions. Ion exchange resins display higher removal efficiency for short-chain PFAS compared to carbon-based sorbents such as GAC and PAC, since the adsorption process is a governed by both hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions. Polymers, natural materials such as minerals, soil, and sediments, have also been used in various studies as sorbents. However, their removal efficiency, especially for short-chain PFAS, remains limited. The meta-analysis conducted in this study showed that there is a lack of research on the removal of the emerging PFAS, and most studies focus mainly on the treatment of long-chain PFAS, especially PFOS and PFOA. Information collected for the evaluation of the adsorption per- formance of ACs and IER ( Tables S1 eS2) and non-conventional materials ( Tables 1 e10) includes: i) type of PFAS tested, ii) sorp- tion ef ﬁciency, iii) tested initial concentrations (C 0) of PFAS and of the adsorbents, and iv) time required to reach adsorption equilib- rium (eq. time). Sorption ef ﬁciency is commonly evaluated by applying adsorption isotherm models and kinetic laws. The former are used to describe the interaction between adsorbent and adsorbate at equilibrium and at constant temperature [110,111]. The Langmuir and Freundlich isotherms are the most widely applied models used to describe the adsorption of organic pollutants on solid materials. Kinetic models to describe sorption kinetics are usually modelled by means of pseudo- ﬁrst and pseudo-second order (PFO and PSO) rate laws [ 112]. Collectively, kinetic models and isotherm models can be used to derive the amount of adsorbed substance at equilibrium (q e) and the maximum amount of adsorbable substance (Q m). Additional information on kinetics, isotherms, and derived parameters of the most used models are available in the SI-part 1.

Final considerations This review consolidated over 130 studies on PFAS remediation in natural waters and showed that no single unit process is universally sufficient, especially for short-chain compounds. Adsorption remains widely applied and is effective mainly for long-chain PFAS due to hy - drophobic interactions, but its performance for short chains is more limited and strongly matrix-dependent. The chromium-plating wastewater first underwent a reduction- sedimentation process to remove Cr, then was mixed with other wastewaters and entered the biochemical system. Conclusions The anion-exchange resin IRA910 was found to be e ﬀective for the removal of PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS, PFHxA, PFBS, and PFBA with high adsorption capacity. Although the IRA910 had high adsorption capacity for all six PFASs, their competitive adsorption was completely di ﬀerent. When PFHxS co-existed with other PFASs in bisolute system, it replaced the adsorbed PFASs with shorter C-F chains on the IRA910, while PFASs with longer C-F chain such as PFOS was not replaced by PFHxS. When six PFASs were presented in the simulated AFFF-impacted groundwater, their adsorbed amounts decreased in the order of PFOS > PFHxS > PFOA > PFBS > PFHxA > PFBA, closely related to their hydrophobicity and functional groups. The nonionic organic compounds including TEC and MB hardly interfered with the PFHxS removal, while ionic ones including SDS and HA signi ﬁcantly decreased the adsorbed amount. The presence of inorganic anions including sul- fate, bicarbonate, chloride, and phosphate slightly decreased the re- moval e ﬃ ciency of PFHxS and their in ﬂuences were almost similar.

Although PFAS sorption is known to depend on the properties of solid matrices, the roles of organic matter and iron (hydr)oxides remain poorly understood, especially for polyfluorinated compounds. To investigate the interplay between particulate organic matter and iron (hydr)oxides in PFAS-contaminated subsurface environments, we studied the partitioning of neutral, cationic, and anionic PFAS in AFFF to well-characterized solids using the mixed- mode solid-phase extraction (SPE) technique combined with the total oxidizable precursor (TOP) assay. In contrast, the effect of goethite, a representative iron-containing mineral, on PFAS sorption varied with the PFAS charge.

Similar to sensor research, the selectivity of sorbents is crucial but hard to compare as it is greatly impacted by the experimental conditions. Furthermore, few papers of PFAS sorbents demonstrated and discussed the selectivity by comparing the adsorption performance between PFAS and its interferents individually; instead, most of them examined the selectivity as the anti-interferent ability by showing an una ﬀected PFAS adsorption performance in the presence of interferents. This method is not unreasonable in terms of demonstrating the selectivity, but at the same time, one should pay attention to the dosage of sorbents, the species of selected interferents, and the concentrations of all analytes in sample solutions and make sure the una ﬀected performance is not caused by overloading of sorbents or using unrealistic sample solutions. Since the adsorption performance is largely related to the initial concentration of PFAS analyte, all sorbents should be tested under environmentally relevant PFAS concentrations (ng/L to μg/L). However, most existing research conducted adsorption experiments in batch mode under unrealistic initial concentrations (>mg/L), 36,115 which cannot truly re ﬂect the capability of those sorbents in real applications. Furthermore, the performance of more sorbents, especially emerging ones, needs to be tested in the column mode, which is a closer proxy to practical environments.

The highly non-polar perfluorinated tails of PFASs are strongly repelled by water, leading to their preferential inter - action with hydrophobic adsorbent surfaces such as AC and certain polymers. This process is facilitated by van der Waals and dispersion forces, and is particularly effective for long- chain PFASs with greater surface areas (Mohona et al. 2023). Electro stati c inter actions Electrostatic attraction is critical in PFAS adsorption when the adsorbent surface carries a positive charge, such as functionalised biochar or ion-exchange resins. The negatively charged PFAS head groups are attracted to the positively charged sites on the adsorbents, enhancing the adsorption process. This mechanism is particularly efficient under near-neutral to slightly acidic pH conditions (Wu C et al. 2020; Kim et al. 2024). These resins possess functional groups (e.g. quaternary ammonium) that are capable of exchanging with PFAS anions in the solution. Therefore, this study aims to pro - vide a critical review of treatment methods and their application in the remediation of PFAS-contaminated aqueous matrices. Additionally, both individual and hybrid treatment processes will be assessed, with a particular focus on the role of MSP as a key process in the development of composite technologies for PFAS remediation. Existing reviews have emphasized either emerging membrane ma - terials without systematically discussing the commercially available ones or focused primarily on high-pressure separations (nanofiltration and reverse osmosis [21] ) without integrating modified micro- and ul - trafiltration or downstream concentrate handling. A review centered on mixed-matrix membranes have additionally been scoped to wastewater applications [22] . In contrast, the present review consolidates perfor - mance data for commercially available and modified membranes and interprets rejection efficiency under environmentally relevant matrices (surface water vs. groundwater), accounting for natural organic matter, divalent cations, ionic strength, and fouling/adsorption mechanisms. It further links upstream separation performance to concentrate-management options and integration with destructive pro - cesses, enabling a coherent view of treatment trains rather than isolated unit operations. Introduction The raw water used for drinking water production contains a variety of natural substances and contaminants originating from pollution in source areas, particularly in downstream catchment zones. Contami - nants of emerging concern (CECs) require special attention, as they have been detected in most aquatic environments [1] . The group of CECs is extensive and includes pharmaceuticals, personal care product in - gredients, pesticides, flame retardants, per- and polyfluoroalkyl sub - stances (PFAS), and disinfection by-products, among others. Given the diverse health and environmental risks associated with CECs, their removal at drinking water treatment plants (DWTPs) is essential.

While existing studies mainly focus on the effectiveness of NF and RO membranes for PFAS removal, the role of UF membranes as a pretreatment step has not yet been sufficiently inves - tigated, especially in real TWW matrices. The present study fills this gap by investigating the performance of a two-stage UF-RO system under low-pressure conditions and analyzing how membrane fouling, water chemistry, and membrane characteristics affect PFAS removal. In contrast to previous studies, which mainly used synthetic wastewater, this research provides insight into the behavior of PFAS in real TWW, where organics, surfactants, and anions such as chlorides and sulfates can affect removal efficiency. In addition, advanced analytical tech - niques such as atomic force microscopy (AFM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) were used to characterize structural and chemical changes in the membranes before and after treatment to gain a deeper understanding of how the surface properties of the membranes affect PFAS removal. While most existing studies on PFAS removal focus on synthetic water matrices or spiked solutions and emphasize the performance of NF and RO, there is still a significant knowledge gap regarding the behavior of PFAS in complex, real industrial wastewater.
